Findings.Comment: The diff deletes `defer resp.Body.Close()` from `WhoAmI`, and the new file has no other `Close` call. On every request, `c.http.Do(req)` hands back a response whose body is read by `json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&u)` (or never read at all on the non-2xx path at line 21) and then abandoned. For a standard `http.Client`, an unclosed body keeps the underlying connection checked out, leaking a connection/FD per call until the process runs out of sockets — this triggers on any successful or failed whoami lookup, not an edge case.
Findings.Headline: Removed defer leaves the whoami response body unclosed

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: Removing `defer resp.Body.Close()` leaks the HTTP response body on every call. Once `c.http.Do(req)` succeeds, neither the success path (`return &u, nil`) nor the non-2xx error path ever closes `resp.Body`. In Go an unclosed body prevents the underlying TCP connection from being returned to the keep-alive pool and leaks the socket until GC, so any caller invoking `WhoAmI` repeatedly (e.g. per request authenticating a token) accumulates leaked connections and file descriptors.

Findings.Comment: Removing the `q.mu.Lock()` / `q.mu.Unlock()` around `q.depth = len(q.pending)` leaves this write unguarded while `Submit` appends to `q.pending` and writes `q.depth` under the mutex and `Depth()` reads `q.depth` under the mutex. Once the worker goroutine is running, a job submitted while a review is in flight hits `Submit` concurrently with this post-`run` update: both goroutines touch `q.pending`/`q.depth` with only one holding the lock, which is a data race in the Go memory model. Realistic outcome is torn or stale `Depth()` values, and `-race` builds will fail outright. The read of `q.pending` on the same line is equally unguarded against `append` in `Submit`.
Findings.Headline: Unlocked write to q.depth in worker races with Submit and Depth

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: The mutex guard around `q.depth = len(q.pending)` was removed from `worker`, so this write now races with the locked writes in `Submit` (`q.depth = len(q.pending)` under `q.mu`) and the locked read in `Depth()`. As soon as a caller submits a job while a worker is finishing `q.run(j)`, the goroutines touch `q.depth` concurrently — a Go data race with undefined behavior (stale/torn depth reports, and fatal failures under the race detector). The unlocked read of `q.pending` on the same line races with `Submit`'s `append` for the same reason.

A realistic run has `Submit` called from a request goroutine while `worker` is finishing a job: the worker reads `q.pending` and writes `q.depth` concurrently with `Submit`'s append/`q.depth = len(...)` and with `Depth`'s `return q.depth`, which is a data race on both the slice header and the int. Under the Go race detector this fails immediately; without it the counter can be stale or torn and `Depth()` returns a wrong backlog.

Findings.Comment: `worker` now writes `q.depth = len(q.pending)` after `q.run(j)` without holding `q.mu`, while `Submit` and `Depth` both read and write `q.depth` and `q.pending` under the mutex. Once the queue is running, a concurrent `Submit(j)` (which appends to `q.pending` and rewrites `q.depth`) or a `Depth()` call races with this unlocked write: the goroutine can publish a stale `len(q.pending)`, clobber a just-submitted job's depth update, or trip the race detector. The previous code bracketed this assignment with `q.mu.Lock()`/`q.mu.Unlock()`; the diff removed both sides of that guard and left the update unprotected.

Findings.Comment: `Depth()` reads `q.depth` under `q.mu`, and `Submit` writes it under `q.mu`, but the worker's post-job update now writes `q.depth` (and reads `q.pending`) with no lock held. Once the worker starts running, any concurrent `Submit` or `Depth` call from another goroutine races with this write: under the Go race detector this is a hard failure, and without it callers can observe a torn or stale backlog depth — exactly the value `Depth` exists to report accurately.

Findings.Comment: The new fallback is unreachable for provider failures: `return this.refresh(base);` returns the promise without awaiting it, so a rejection from `provider.fetch` propagates out of the async `getRates` without ever entering `catch (err)`. Trigger: cache holds an expired table, `provider.fetch` rejects → `getRates` throws instead of serving the expired table and incrementing `staleServed`, which is the behavior this diff exists to add. `refresh` only throws asynchronously (it awaits `provider.fetch` and `cache.set`), so the `catch` block is dead code in every realistic failure path. Awaiting the call makes the rejection surface at the `try` and lets the stale-serving path run.
Findings.Headline: Stale-fallback catch never fires: refresh promise is not awaited

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: `return this.refresh(base)` inside the `try` hands the rejected promise straight to the caller: `catch` only sees synchronous throws, and `refresh` is `async`, so every provider failure becomes a rejection that bypasses the `catch` entirely. Concrete path: cache holds an expired table → `getRates` is called → `provider.fetch` rejects → `refresh` returns a rejected promise → `catch (err)` never runs → `getRates` rejects and the request fails. The documented behavior ("that table is served rather than failing the request"), the `staleServed` counter, and the `logger.warn` call are all unreachable. Awaiting the call inside the `try` routes the rejection into the `catch` as intended.
Findings.Headline: Stale-rate fallback never runs: returned promise rejects outside the try

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: The `catch` around `this.refresh(base)` covers the whole refresh sequence, not just `provider.fetch`: `refresh` also runs `this.cache.set(...)` and `this.logger.info(...)`. If the provider succeeds but the cache write throws (e.g. cache backend briefly unavailable), the freshly fetched table is discarded, `staleServed` is incremented, and `logger.warn` reports "rate provider failed" — so the metric and log both attribute a cache failure to the provider, and callers get stale rates while fresh ones were actually obtained. This contradicts both the doc comment above `getRates` ("when the provider fails") and the `staleServedCount` doc ("because the provider failed"). Narrow the catch to the fetch step, or widen the docs/metric wording to cover cache failures.
Findings.Headline: Stale fallback also masks cache-write failures, miscounting them as provider failures

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Matches.Why: finding on src/rates/rate-service.ts:73 mentions none of [await never catch not caught never run rejection unreachable]

Findings.Comment: `getRates` wraps `this.refresh(base)` in a `try`/`catch` but returns the promise without awaiting it inside the `try`. `refresh` is an `async` method, so it never throws synchronously — it always returns a promise, and a failure from `this.provider.fetch(base)` surfaces as that promise rejecting. The `return` statement does not await it, so the rejection propagates straight out of `getRates` and the `catch` block is never entered: the intended stale-table fallback (`return cached`), the `staleServed` counter, and the warn log are all unreachable. Realistic scenario: the provider is down and an expired table is cached — the caller still receives a rejection instead of the cached rates, which is exactly the failure this change set out to prevent.

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: `getRates` wraps `this.refresh(base)` in a `try/catch` and returns the promise without `await`. `refresh` is an `async` method, so when `provider.fetch` (or `cache.set`) rejects, `this.refresh(base)` itself does not throw — it returns a rejected promise, which `return` hands straight out of `getRates`. The `catch` block therefore never runs: the stale-table fallback, the `staleServed` increment, and the warn log are dead code, and a request made while the provider is down and the cached table is expired fails with the provider error instead of being served stale rates as the doc comment on `getRates` promises. The classic `return p` vs `return await p` try/catch pitfall; `staleServedCount` will also stay 0 forever.

Findings.Comment: The commit error is now discarded and `AddClaim` returns `nil` unconditionally. If the transaction fails to commit (connection loss, serialization failure, constraint deferred to commit time), the caller is told the claim was recorded when nothing was persisted, and `defer tx.Rollback(ctx)` on an already-closed transaction is a no-op that cannot recover the failure. The previous code surfaced this error; swallowing it silently converts a failed write into a reported success.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim discards the commit error and always reports success

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: `AddClaim` now discards the error returned by `tx.Commit(ctx)` and unconditionally returns `nil`. A commit can fail after the `INSERT` succeeds (deferred constraint violation, serialization failure, connection loss at commit time), and in that case the caller is told the claim was recorded while nothing was persisted. Any caller that proceeds on `nil` — e.g. treating the project as owned by the team, or skipping a retry — will operate on a claim that does not exist. The previous code checked the commit error and surfaced it; this change silently converts a failed write into a success.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim ignores commit error and reports success unconditionally

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: This change discards the return value of `tx.Commit(ctx)`, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success. A realistic path: `INSERT` succeeds on a connection where the transaction later fails to commit (serialization failure, deferred constraint violation on `team_claims`, or the connection dropping between exec and commit) — `AddClaim` then returns `nil`, and the caller records the project as claimed while nothing was persisted. The prior code wrapped and returned the commit error; dropping that check turns a transient database failure into silent data loss. Note also that the deferred `tx.Rollback` cannot recover anything here: after a failed commit the transaction is already aborted, and its error is ignored as well.
Findings.Headline: Commit error in AddClaim is silently discarded

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: The commit error is now discarded, so a failed commit (serialization failure, constraint violation deferred to commit, connection loss) is reported to the caller as success. A caller that proceeds after `AddClaim` returns nil will believe the team owns the project when no row was committed — silent data loss on the claim record. The deleted code returned this error; restoring the check is required.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim discards the transaction commit error

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: Dropping the error check on `tx.Commit(ctx)` means a failed commit is silently swallowed and `AddClaim` returns `nil` to the caller. Realistic path: the insert succeeds inside the transaction, but the commit fails (serialization failure, deferred constraint violation, connection loss to Postgres) — the caller records the claim as persisted, the row is never written, and no error is surfaced anywhere. This is the exact case the removed `return fmt.Errorf("commit claim: %w", err)` existed to catch.

Findings.Comment: The two error values in `Store.Owner` are swapped: the `errNoRows` branch now wraps the raw scan error while a genuine database fault is reported as `ErrNoClaim`. A caller that checks `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` to decide "this project is unowned, I can claim it" will now treat a connection failure or timeout as an unowned project and proceed to claim it, while a legitimately unowned project fails the check and is rejected. This also contradicts the function's own doc comment ("Callers distinguish 'nobody owns it' from a database fault with errors.Is"), which is now inverted. Restore the original mapping: no-rows → `ErrNoClaim`, any other error → wrap `err`.
Findings.Headline: Store.Owner swaps ErrNoClaim and scan error between branches

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.

Findings.Comment: The two error returns are swapped, inverting the contract documented two lines above (`Callers distinguish "nobody owns it" from a database fault with errors.Is`). On a realistic input — a project key with no row in `team_claims` — `Scan` returns `errNoRows`, but the code now wraps that raw driver error instead of `ErrNoClaim`, so `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` is false and callers treat a missing claim as an unknown/DB failure. Conversely, a genuine pool/network fault now returns an error satisfying `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)`, so a database outage is reported as "project has no owner", which can lead to silent misattribution of ownership. The error-to-return mapping is reversed in both branches.

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.

Findings.Comment: The two error returns were swapped. On the no-row path the code now wraps `err` (pgx's `ErrNoRows`) instead of `ErrNoClaim`, so a caller doing `errors.Is(err, store.ErrNoClaim)` to detect an unclaimed project gets false and instead sees a raw driver error. Conversely, the real-fault branch (connection failure, query error) wraps `ErrNoClaim`, so `errors.Is(err, store.ErrNoClaim)` returns true and the caller treats a database outage as "this project has no owner" — that path can silently grant or report ownership where none exists. Findings.Comment: The two error returns in `Owner` are swapped relative to the documented contract: the `errors.Is(err, errNoRows)` branch (no row exists, i.e. nobody owns the project) now wraps the raw `err`, while the branch for actual database faults wraps `ErrNoClaim`. On a query failure callers doing `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` will conclude the project is unowned and may let another team claim it, and on a genuinely unowned project they will see an unexpected error instead of `ErrNoClaim`, contradicting both `ErrNoClaim`'s doc comment ("what callers match on when a project has no owner yet") and `Owner`'s ("Callers distinguish 'nobody owns it' from a database fault with errors.Is").

Findings.Comment: This diff swaps the two error returns so the semantics are inverted: a missing claim now wraps the raw `pgx` no-rows error, while a genuine database fault is reported as `ErrNoClaim`. Realistic scenario: the DB connection drops or the query fails mid-request — `Scan` returns a non-no-rows error, the second branch runs, and the caller's `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` check succeeds, so the project is treated as unowned (or the caller wrongly offers a claim path) instead of surfacing the fault. Conversely, when nobody owns the project, callers matching on `ErrNoClaim` no longer see it and will treat a normal "no owner" case as an unexpected error. This directly contradicts the doc comment above the function ("Callers distinguish 'nobody owns it' from a database fault with errors.Is") and the exported `ErrNoClaim` contract.
